title: Photo-transformable additive and resonant SAM molecule tackle two perovskite stability problems at once
content:
Photo-transformable additive and resonant SAM molecule tackle two perovskite stability problems at once
Researchers connected to Chinese flexible-perovskite maker
have published two separate papers within the same month, addressing two of the field's persistent stability problems: halide segregation in wide-bandgap perovskite/organic tandems, and desorption of the self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) used at the perovskite/electrode interface.
The first paper, from researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Shanghai Jiao Tong University - including SunFlex co-founder and CAS academician Yongfang Li - tackles a known weakness of wide-bandgap, high-bromide mixed-halide perovskites, which are used as the front cell in perovskite/organic tandem solar cells: they tend to mix unevenly during crystallization and undergo light-induced halide segregation during operation, both of which limit device performance. The team introduced a photo-transformable additive, 4-[3-(trifluoromethyl)-3H-diazirin-3-yl]benzylamine (TDB), into the perovskite precursor solution to address both problems in sequence. During crystallization, TDB suppresses the rapid precipitation of the bromide-rich phase and speeds up halide mixing during annealing, improving initial homogeneity. Then, once the device is under illumination, TDB itself transforms into a new chemical species that adsorbs more strongly onto the perovskite's grain-boundary surfaces, blocking the formation of iodide-related defects and suppressing both defect-assisted carrier trapping and ion migration - the mechanisms behind light-induced halide segregation.
Applied to a wide-bandgap perovskite cell (1.88 eV bandgap), the strategy produced a single-junction device with a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 20.01%, an open-circuit voltage of 1.42 V, and a fill factor of 85.13%, along with improved stability under illumination. Built into a full monolithic perovskite/organic tandem cell, the technology reached a PCE of 28.80%, with a certified steady-state efficiency of 28.04%. The tandem retained 90% of its initial PCE after 625 hours of operation under the ISOS-L-1 stability testing protocol.
The second paper, from researchers at Soochow University, Southeast University and Hangzhou Dianzi University, addresses SAMs, which anchor to the transparent conductive oxide (TCO) substrate and form an interfacial dipole that helps extract charge carriers from the perovskite layer - a technique that has driven a series of efficiency gains in perovskite solar cells. The problem is that SAM molecules typically bond to the substrate only weakly, since their coordination sites have limited electron density, making them prone to desorbing under operational stress and compromising long-term stability. The team's solution was a new SAM built around a donor-acceptor-donor (D-A-D) resonant molecular structure, in which electronic resonance effects increase the negative charge density at the anchoring group, substantially strengthening the bond between its phosphonic acid group and the indium tin oxide (ITO) substrate and preventing desorption during operation.
Devices built with the new SAM showed negligible performance decay under maximum-power-point tracking at 85±5°C for 1,080 hours, retained over 93% of their initial efficiency after 1,080 hours under metal-halide lamp illumination (100 mW/cm², with 4.4% UV content) at 85±5°C, and retained over 98% of their initial efficiency after 720 thermal cycles between -40°C and 85°C. The same charge delocalization effect that strengthens the anchoring bond also improves carrier transport, and the devices reached certified efficiencies of 27.69% on small (0.063 cm²) rigid devices, 23.63% on a larger 15.64 cm² aperture area, and 26.64% on flexible substrates - the team highlighting that last result as evidence the approach works across both rigid and flexible device types.
Together, the two papers represent a significant show of research output for a single company-linked team within one month, following on from SunFlex's other recent moves, including a strategic partnership with aerospace company Nayuta Space to develop a 400 m² rollable flexible perovskite solar sail for satellites.

title: 三项光伏能耗能效强制性国标明年1月起正式实施-索比光伏网
content:
从国家标准委了解到，三项光伏领域能耗能效强制性国家标准明年一月起正式实施，三项标准将从源头严控低效产品入市、推动光伏产业技术迭代与绿色升级。
在生产企业能源消耗控制方面，《硅单晶单位产品能源消耗限额》和《硅多晶和锗单位产品能源消耗限额》两项强制性国家标准，聚焦光伏组件核心原材料，统一能耗统计范围和计算方法。在产品能源效率提升方面，《晶体硅光伏组件和逆变器能效限定值及能效等级》强制性国家标准，对地面电站、工商业及户用光伏等场景用光伏组件和逆变器划定能效等级。
中国标准化研究院资源环境所研究员夏玉娟介绍：
能效一级是行业的标杆水平，性能最优，持续引领技术升级;
能效二级是高效产品;
能效三级是产品进入市场的最低门槛。
达不到三级的产品，一律禁止生产、进口和销售。
三项光伏领域强制性国家标准的发布实施，将全面压实光伏全产业链节能降碳要求，倒逼低效落后产能有序退出。

title: How Meta Plans to Close the Gap with Anthropic and OpenAI in Coding
content: As Meta Platforms races to catch up with Anthropic and OpenAI , it’s asking thousands of engineers to use its in-house AI coding agent, MetaCode , in their day-to-day work in an effort to improve the coding capabilities of its AI models. Maher Saba , vice president of Meta’s Applied AI Engineering organization, last month asked engineers across the company to write at least one code “diff” a week— a code change that is reviewed and integrated into the models, according to an internal memo reviewed by The Information. When the model gets something wrong, they’re encouraged to fix it and submit those corrections. Saba said engineers’ use and feedback on MetaCode has already helped boost the coding capabilities of the latest version of Meta's AI model, Muse Spark 1.1 , and those same corrections will be used to post-train an upcoming model dubbed “Watermelon” internally. Meta isn’t just hoping to close the gap between its AI models and those of its rivals. The company is also trying to reduce its reliance on pricey external coding tools , such as Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex , after spending billions of dollars on those products this year. Anthropic’s Claude Code has become one of the most widely adopted coding assistants among enterprises, and Meta is among a growing list of companies looking for ways to control the rising cost of AI tools . By asking engineers to make at least one coding change a week, the effort goes beyond the kind of product “dogfooding” common across the tech industry, where companies including Google , Microsoft and OpenAI encourage employees to use their own AI products. Meta is also gamifying the push, awarding engineers different-colored badges on their internal profile pages based on the number of coding changes they contribute. The effort appears to be gaining traction inside Meta. MetaCode now has roughly 7,000 weekly active users and employee corrections have led to more than 800 fixes to the system, Saba said in the memo. Those improvements have also helped boost MetaCode’s score on the DeepSWE software engineering benchmark, according to the memo. A Meta spokesperson referred The Information to a statement the company has previously given: “It’s well-known that this is a priority, and we’re focused on using AI to help employees with their day-to-day work.” Meta’s internal push also raises the question of whether the company plans to eventually release MetaCode publicly, as CEO Mark Zuckerberg has hinted. On Meta’s second-quarter earnings call last week, he said the company has “more coding and productivity tools on our roadmap as well.” The popularity of coding products from Anthropic and OpenAI has made them difficult competitors to dislodge. Open-source coding models have also become increasingly capable, adding pressure on Meta to build its own alternative. title: ByteDance’s Founder Rules Out Distillation on AI Models
content: ByteDance won’t resort to distillation as a shortcut to advancing its AI model capabilities, even if that means the company lags behind domestic rivals for now, founder Zhang Yiming told employees during a meeting last month. One reason, say people close to the company, is ByteDance’s complicated history with the U.S. government over the company’s TikTok video app. The previously unreported comments, heard by two employees present at the meeting, offer a rare glimpse into the ByteDance founder’s thinking on the company’s AI development strategy. The meeting, an all-hands for ByteDance’s AI team internally known as Seed, took place just after Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 model sparked alarms in the U.S. that Chinese models were narrowing the gap at a pace quicker than previously expected. In the weeks since, a senior White House official has accused Kimi K3 of achieving better performance by distilling U.S. frontier models. (Distillation is the process of training a new model using outputs from existing, most advanced models.) The caution against distillation stems from the company’s experiences with TikTok, which the U.S. government threatened to ban multiple times over national security concerns, according to one of the employees and another person with knowledge of ByteDance’s internal discussions. TikTok’s existential crisis was resolved last year after a deal was reached to sell the vast majority of TikTok’s U.S. data security operation to a group of U.S.-led investors. But ByteDance continues to run the commercial operations of TikTok globally, including the U.S. And the company worries that distilling U.S. frontier models would set off a new wave of scrutiny from Washington and pose new threats to TikTok, according to the employee and the person with knowledge of ByteDance’s internal discussions. Zhang, who rarely spoke at the Seed team’s previous meetings, broke his silence after other leaders talked about why the company won’t use distillation to get ahead. ByteDance “should be willing to sacrifice some short-term gains for longer-term goals,” Zhang said, without elaborating what the long-term goals are, according to the employees. ByteDance’s reluctance to use distillation has been seen as a reason for why its large language models are trailing other AI labs in China, including Alibaba and upstarts like DeepSeek, Z.ai and Moonshot, according to the employees. In contrast, ByteDance is widely recognized as a global leader in AI video generation models, following the success of its Seedance 2.0 model, which made shockwaves earlier this year for its ability to produce hyperrealistic videos. ByteDance has increasingly become an oddity in China’s AI landscape, partly because the social media giant is the only major Chinese AI firm whose LLMs are almost all proprietary models, while its peers focus on open-source models. ByteDance’s flagship LLMs are not always included in major global LLM leaderboards, a common window for outsiders to track model capabilities. Customers access ByteDance’s models mainly through the company’s cloud computing platform, which has a smaller market share in China than industry leaders Alibaba, Huawei and Tencent. This makes it difficult for non-customers to gauge how good ByteDance’s models are. ByteDance’s latest LLM, Seed 2.1 Pro, is not seen on Artificial Analysis, the most widely followed leaderboard. The model ranks No. 19 on Arena AI’s coding leaderboard for web development, far below other Chinese models. Inside ByteDance’s Seed team, there have long been ongoing debates about whether the company should turn to distillation, according to the ByteDance employees. This year, rapid advancements of open-source models from domestic rivals have created more pressure for ByteDance. Every time a new powerful Chinese open-source model dropped, ByteDance’s internal debates about distillation heated up, according to the employees. Distillation has become a sensitive and highly controversial topic due to the intensifying AI rivalry between the U.S. and China. Trump administration officials have long criticized Chinese AI developers for allegedly using distillation to copy the capabilities of leading models from Anthropic and OpenAI. Anthropic has accused many Chinese AI firms—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax, Z.ai and Alibaba—of illicitly extracting Claude’s capabilities through large-scale distillation to improve their own models. Anthropic, however, hasn’t made such an accusation against ByteDance. The accused Chinese firms haven’t publicly commented about the distillation allegations. To be sure, developers in the U.S. have also credited the Chinese AI firms with making their own technical advances to improve their models. Distillation alone cannot explain the strong performance of China’s best open-source models such as Moonshot’s Kimi K3, which rivals the best U.S. models on some benchmarks, they said. DeepSeek, for example, is widely recognized for its architectural innovations that drastically lower memory requirements during model training and inference. But researchers at Chinese AI firms also acknowledge that distillation does bring significant advantages. It saves a lot of training time and computation overhead because a new model under development can learn directly from the reasoning steps of an existing frontier model, instead of relying solely on raw and curated training data, they say.

title: China’s New AI Gold Rush: World Models
content: When Hongyuan Lu finished his doctorate program in AI and engineering a year ago, he reached out to some investors to see if he could raise money for a startup to build world models, AI systems that can understand and simulate the physical world. But the investors, who were focusing on AI agent apps at the time, weren’t interested. This year, the environment is completely different, he said. “World model” has become a new buzz phrase in China’s startup sector, and Lu, who has co-authored academic papers exploring how to make AI understand a virtual spatial environment, started receiving friend requests on the WeChat messaging app from venture capitalists. His startup—FaceMind, which is based in Shanghai and Hong Kong—has raised $20 million in seed money this year from investors including Chinese cybersecurity firm Qihoo 360’s venture fund. “If I work for big companies, I may not have the freedom to explore world models, because those companies have their own strategies and many other priorities,” said Lu, who turned down a job offer from ByteDance to work on FaceMind. Lu is one of a huge number of Chinese entrepreneurs, including many university professors or doctoral students, rushing to launch their own AI labs. And while that trend is replicated in the U.S. to some degree, more U.S. neolabs tend to focus on diverse research labs and are run by researchers who have spent time at or even held executive positions at established companies. What’s different about this new generation of Chinese AI labs is that they’re mostly focused on world models, which simulate real-world environments and aim to approximate the physics of how objects move and interact with the surroundings. That’s because world models are considered the key to unlocking breakthroughs in humanoids and autonomous vehicles, two areas where China has the world’s broadest and deepest supply chain. The Chinese neolabs think they have a shot, because the race to build world models is still in the early stage, with no front-runners yet, in contrast with the well-beaten path of large language models. Local venture capitalists say that has produced a frenzy of interest in world models reminiscent of the large language model boom in 2023, when countless new Chinese startups raced to develop large language models in what local media described as the “war of 100 models.” “The hype around world models right now is unprecedented. Big tech companies, startups and venture investors are all rushing in,” said Jianke Zhang, a second-year AI and robotics doctoral student at Tsinghua University, who co-founded world model startup LatentVerse with his classmate two months ago. “There are so many Ph.D. students launching their own startups now,” Zhang said. LatentVerse raised tens of millions of dollars in June from blue-chip investors like Hillhouse and is now looking at raising a new round of funding. The gold rush is so intense that all kinds of startups are starting to adopt the world model label based on their own interpretation of the concept. For instance, PettiChat, a Chinese startup founded in January that develops wearable AI devices for pets, said in April that it is building what will be the first “animal behavior world model,” an AI system aimed at simulating and predicting a pet’s behavior. Researchers launching their own startups for world models this year have a new formula for raising money, which they’ve dubbed “1-3-5-7.” That means they want to be valued at $100 million in their first funding round, $300 million in their second, and so forth. Some of them are even raising the first three rounds in the same discussion, asking investors to commit to all of them. Some venture capitalists caution it could be a risky bet to invest in researchers who lack the track record of building frontier models at established labs or tech companies. By comparison, many U.S. neolab founders are researchers who have spent time or even held executive positions at established companies such as OpenAI and xAI . The list of challenges for Chinese neolabs doesn’t stop here. All of them face a congenital weakness: a shortage of advanced chips, imposed by U.S. export restrictions. Skeptics say the Chinese neolabs will struggle to secure enough chips and talent, once the hype wears off. While newly founded world model startups are quickly raising money, they will have to compete with deep-pocketed tech giants and well-established AI unicorns for limited chip supplies. Major Chinese AI firms Moonshot AI and DeepSeek, both of which have raised billions of dollars from investors, used Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips to train their most recent large language models, as The Information reported. Researchers at new Chinese startups working on world models say they are renting chips from tech giants that operate cloud services, such as Alibaba and Baidu, to train the models. But they also acknowledge that most Chinese neolabs haven’t found a long-term solution for the compute problem. War of 100 World Models In the U.S., a few new world model startups founded by well-known AI pioneers have raised billions of dollars. World Labs, a San Francisco–based startup led by Stanford professor Fei-Fei Li, a pioneer in spatial intelligence research, raised $1 billion at a $5 billion valuation in February. In March, former Meta Platforms chief AI scientist Yann LeCun raised more than $1 billion in a seed round for his new startup, Advanced Machine Intelligence Labs. What’s happening in the U.S. has sparked intense discussion in China’s tech and investment circles about the importance of world models as the critical step toward large-scale commercialization of humanoids and other automation technologies. The concept of world models resonates particularly strongly in China because the country has massive manufacturing and logistics industries, which provide real-world data from factories and warehouses, as well as strong government support for robotics. One of the world model startups attracting a lot of attention from investors in recent months is Ziran Yizhi—“natural will” in English. Its founder, Ning Ding, an assistant professor at Tsinghua University, was the main author of a highly influential 2023 academic paper about a technique to fine-tune massive AI models by updating a tiny fraction of their parameters. The Beijing-based startup, founded earlier this year, is valued at about $570 million, and its backers include HongShan, Ant Group and battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd., according to a person with knowledge of the matter. A growing number of established companies from traditional industries are also backing world model startups. Last week, Shenzhen Edge Medical, a Hong Kong–listed medical device company, announced that it has invested in PrimalVerse, a Beijing-based world model startup founded in January by another assistant professor of Tsinghua University. Shenzhen Edge Medical said in a regulatory filing that it will work with the startup to develop AI-powered surgical robots. Some Chinese AI unicorns that develop video-generation models have shifted their focus to world models. Beijing-based ShengShu Technology used to be best known for its AI video business, Vidu, which competes with ByteDance’s Seedance video models. In April, ShengShu released Motubrain, a world model that aims to serve as the brain for robots to navigate the physical environment. Shengshu now describes itself as a “general world model company.” In January, PixVerse, another AI video-generation startup that competes with ShengShu, launched a “real-time world model,” R1, which allows users to create a realistic virtual world and keep making changes to it in real time, all with text or image prompts. Earlier this month, PixVerse announced PixVerse Game Engine, a new software framework powered by the R1 model for building interactive videogames. While some investors are starting to describe the world model movement as a bubble, founders say the rapid concentration of capital and resources could lead to real advancements. “Without this bubble, it may not be possible for breakthroughs to happen,” Zhang said.

title: SpaceX Reports Lots of Red Ink and Makes Big Promises
content: Question: How is the 24-year-old SpaceX like a young startup? It’s burning twice as much cash as it brings in as revenue! That’s one takeaway from SpaceX’s first earnings report as a public company, in which the company revealed it burned $16 billion in the second quarter, on $7.8 billion in revenue. That’s thanks to a whopping $18.4 billion in capital expenditures, mostly due to SpaceX’s AI data center expansion. And like a young startup, SpaceX has big ambitions. On the company’s earnings call with analysts, CEO Elon Musk claimed it was now expecting to hit $1 trillion in revenue by 2030, a year earlier than it had projected before its IPO, and there was a chance it could hit that threshold by 2029. That’s a big claim, considering that first-half revenue was only $12.5 billion. True, finance chief Bret Johnsen said SpaceX’s annualized revenue rate would hit $100 billion by the end of this year. But ARR is one month’s revenue multiplied by 12. It’s not a real metric (and Musk emphasized that the $1 trillion projection was revenue, not ARR). Musk also claimed that SpaceX’s Starlink could deliver most of the internet connectivity in the world in “less than 10 years,” while his No. 2, Gwynne Shotwell, claimed that SpaceX’s Starlink mobile service—to launch at the end of 2027—would “acquire quite a few” of the customers of the major cellphone providers in the U.S. Whoa! So not only does SpaceX have enormous ambitions to dominate broadband internet, it aims to compete directly with major cellular providers. And that’s all in addition to its huge AI ambitions and its desire to launch data centers in space and travel to far-off planets. Investors seem underwhelmed (or perhaps overwhelmed?) by all these big claims: SpaceX stock fell 6.5% in after-hours trading. The investor reaction makes sense. Investors have come to hate big tech companies’ massive outlays on capex for AI, even though those companies are funding that capex from massive profits on other businesses. And SpaceX is spending more on capex, relative to what its businesses generate in cash, than any big tech firm. SpaceX’s only real profit center is its Starlink internet business, but that makes nowhere near enough to fund all the company’s ambitions (Starlink made just $1.65 billion in second-quarter operating income, for instance). SpaceX will undoubtedly get a lift from the various deals it has done to rent out its computing capacity and from its pending acquisition of AI firm Cursor. But becoming a major competitor in mobile and building more AI capacity won’t come cheap. The returns are questionable, both in AI and telecom. Remember that the big telecom providers have to spend a fortune on spectrum and equipment, and they’re all fighting over a market with little growth. Musk has sky-high ambitions. Watching him try to fulfill them promises to be a lot of fun. Bandwidth Constraints AI has created massive demand for electricity and chips, driving up the prices of both, which has in turn lifted the costs of smartphones and computers. Elon Musk on Tuesday pointed out that the demand for bandwidth to transmit data will also soar as a result of AI. “With the advent of AI and humanoid robotics and vehicle robotics and just a massive number of robots, the appetite of bandwidth will be much greater than it has been in the past,” he told analysts. In other words, all those robots and self-driving cars and AI-enabled devices will be communicating constantly, straining the capacity of broadband providers, which are now mostly cable companies and cell firms. Musk says Starlink will save the day, providing the bandwidth to meet all those demands. In Other News • Italian conglomerate Bending Spoons agreed to buy once high-flying productivity startup Airtable for $1.285 billion, a steep haircut to its last valuation of $11 billion in 2021 ( more here ). • Spotify reported 14% higher revenue, driven by 9% growth in the number of paying subscribers, while the music streaming service’s ad business continued to lag. • The Trump administration is planning to ban U.S. imports of data center components from China, Reuters reported . • Major personal computer makers including HP, Asus and Acer have started using small numbers of chips from Chinese memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies, Nikkei Asia reported . • Polymarket is in early talks to raise about $1 billion at a more than $20 billion valuation, Bloomberg reported . • OpenAI gave a full-throated response to Apple’s lawsuit filed last month alleging theft of trade secrets. In a blog post on Tuesday, OpenAI called the lawsuit “careless, aggressive and oddly personal.” • AMD reported 50% higher revenue of $11.536 billion for the second quarter, driven by stronger demand from data centers for its chips. But the company projected slightly slower growth of 41% for the third quarter. AMD shares fell 8.6% in after-hours trading. title: Inside the Airtable-Bending Spoons Sale
content: What an ending. Airtable, valued at $11 billion in 2021 after a trio of funding rounds in under two years, is being acquired by Italian conglomerate Bending Spoons for just $1.285 billion in cash, the companies said on Tuesday. The price tag for the once-hot productivity app seems like a blow to shareholders, particularly those like hedge fund XN, Thrive Capital and Greenoaks Capital that led its last rounds. And the price, amounting to less than three times annualized revenue, should lower expectations for future sales of enterprise software startups (Airtable was No. 2 on our recent list of such targets .) But there’s more to this deal than meets the eye. Alongside the deal price, Airtable also has around $900 million in cash on its balance sheet that can be distributed to its preferred stockholders. What’s left goes to its common shareholders, according to people with knowledge of the deal. That’s in part due to Airtable CEO Howie Liu’s energetic fundraising, which brought in $1.3 billion over the company’s 14-year history. As a result, many shareholders should at least get back the money they invested, the people said. Earlier investors, such as CRV and Caffeinated Capital, should get a sizable return. There’s more. Bending Spoons is not buying all of Airtable. Six months ago, Airtable launched HyperAgent, its platform for building and deploying AI agents. Just a few days before selling to Bending Spoons, Airtable spun off HyperAgent to a standalone company called HyperAgent Inc., according to an SEC filing and people with knowledge of the deal. Airtable investors will get a stake in HyperAgent, according to the people, though the exact structure, including cost, couldn’t be learned. Liu has also told investors that the new HyperAgent startup will be able to raise its own funding and he plans to run it full-time after the Bending Spoons deal closes, said a person with knowledge of the communications. Of course, just getting the investment back isn’t a great return for later investors. Buying the S&P 500 in September 2020 would have doubled investors’ money. And common stock holders fared worse. Investors who bought common stock in a small secondary transaction in 2021, valued between $5.5 billion and $11 billion, lost money, according to a person with direct knowledge of the situation. “It’s venture; it happens,” the person said. And while employees are getting some money to account for their equity, the sale price is likely a disappointment. Bain Capital Ventures partner Aaref Hilaly estimates there is about $850 million for common shareholders in the deal. If the founders own about 20%, there should be about $127 million left for about 900 employees. “Common shareholders should get something from this, just nowhere near what they were hoping for,” he said on The Information’s TITV streaming show Thursday . He noted the company had been valued at $4 billion recently on secondary-market exchanges. Spokespeople for Airtable and Bending Spoons didn’t respond to requests for comment. Airtable’s reorganization and sale could prove to be a turning point for privately held enterprise software startups. Almost since the last tech bubble collapsed in 2022, venture capitalists have been wrestling with what to do with portfolios full of software startups whose valuations looked far too high given the sell-off in public peers. Mounting competition from AI apps further worsened the outlook for many, slowing revenue growth and pushing founders to hastily remake their startups as AI companies. Airtable’s sale shows one path to the finish line: A deeply discounted price and a fresh start as an AI company. title: How Firms Like Coinbase Are Building Coding Agents to Complement Anthropic's Claude Code
content: Coinbase and some other tech-savvy firms such as Shopify and Ramp have built their own AI coding agents for internal use, giving their employees an alternative to pricey options from firms like Anthropic and OpenAI. Coinbase, the cryptocurrency exchange, built an AI coding agent called Forge, which launched to all of its engineers in April of this year, senior director of engineering Chintan Turakhia told me. Engineers can access the coding agent through Slack, Github, and its own web user interface. Usage of Forge is growing fast internally and has resulted in cost savings, said Turakhia, although he declined to be specific. “There was a time where we didn't have, really, sort of any limits on AI spend, and yes, the spend went up,” he said. But as Forge has become more popular among engineers, “ now our spend has gone down while our token usage continues to go up.” That’s partly because Forge connects to the company’s internal model router to tap different models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and open source model providers to save on cost. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong in a late June post on X said the company has experimented with using Chinese open source models such as GLM 5.2 and Kimi K2.7. He said the company has also used other methods to cut its AI spending “nearly in half,” such as starting new sessions with AI tools to avoid giving the AI too much information to process and thus raising costs. Forge can be tagged in Slack channels, which are essentially large group chats within the messaging app. It can perform tasks like brainstorming ideas for new software features or products and building them. Forge can work inside Coinbase’s code repositories and enterprise software systems such as Datadog and Sentry. Still, Coinbase hasn’t stopped using Anthropic’s Claude Code. In fact, Claude Code is still the most-used AI coding tool used among the 2,500 Coinbase engineers who use such tools, including Cursor and Forge, Turakhia said. “There is no crisp answer on when someone uses Claude Code versus Forge. It depends on the engineer's preferences,” he added. Other companies have figured out how to control their spending on Anthropic’s coding tool by developing internal tools. In this story from last week , I talked about IT firm Globant using an internal coding agent that can swap between models from Anthropic and OpenAI to open source ones for coding work. Then there’s Shopify, whose engineers use its agent River through Slack in addition to Claude Code as well as Codex. Shopify executives said in a May presentation that 75% of its employees use the tool and that it is “very efficient at using tokens,” or doing more coding work at a lower cost. To be sure, sometimes internal AI developments at companies still result in high costs. For example, Walmart had to cap internal usage of its in-house coding agent called Code Puppy after soaring usage, Bloomberg reported in June. Palantir CEO Feeds the AI Fear Fire Palantir CEO Alex Karp has lately been beating the drum about the potential competitive threat AI labs pose to their own customers because they have access to those customers’ proprietary business data. Though OpenAI and Anthropic say they don’t train their AI models on their enterprise customers’ data, there are ways they could use some of those customers’ chat log data to improve their products— an issue my colleagues previously covered in this column. And Anthropic has a history of introducing products that compete with its own partners such as Cursor and Figma. Karp played into the fear factor in his quarterly letter to shareholders Monday: “Every organization in the world is awakening to the risks of handing the creators of the language models the keys to their institutions, of letting the models loose within their homes.” While his warnings have some merit, it’s an all-too-convenient message for Palantir and other software firms, which have seen their stocks fall this year over worries that AI tools could diminish their competitive positions. The companies—Palantir, Microsoft, Salesforce, and others—want to capitalize on recent criticisms of AI labs and position themselves as necessary intermediaries for enterprises. “Our customers have declined to become vassal states of the language labs,” Karp wrote with his characteristic dramatic flair. “And the market is now shifting dramatically underfoot.” Whether the latter will prove true long term remains to be seen, but Palantir certainly appears to be benefiting from popularity among enterprises in the near term, as seen in the record value of contracts it signed in the June quarter with U.S. enterprises . That helped push the stock up nearly 30% on Tuesday. content:
The Download: NASA’s new telescope and Chinese tech import curbs
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
NASA’s new dark energy space telescope can also detect killer asteroids

Read our story about how this new space telescope might boost planetary defense.
—Robin George Andrews
MIT Technology Review Narrated: The inevitable weakness of metrics
—Bryan Gardiner
There are plenty of useful things a metric can reveal. There are even more that it can obscure or corrupt.
Like a lot of people bitten by the self-quantifying bug, I started gathering personal data to pursue a nebulous collection of goals and desires. I wanted to feel better physically and emotionally, get outside more, and bring order to the messiness and uncertainty of my daily existence.
But external metrics and data can never capture what's truly important. Worse, they inevitably redefine your core sense of what's important, whether you're aware of the trap or not. Read the full story.
This is our latest story to be turned into an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

The news comes just after the FCC announced curbs on other high-tech Chinese hardware. (Reuters $)
+ Texas is now requiring data centers to pass an audit before connecting to the grid. (The Verge $)

+ The company’s future plans rely on the success of its huge Starship rockets. (WSJ $)
+ Meanwhile, SpaceX’s spending on AI is soaring. (NYT $)

Including an Anthropic model setting up fake accounts mimicking real people. (BBC)
+ The White House has a new cybersecurity framework…but it’s keeping details under wraps. (Wired $)
+ Here’s why AI agents lie and cheat to reach their goals. (MIT Technology Review)

Turmoil in the US is creating opportunities for European AI that it hopes to seize. (Wired $)
5 People are betting on wildfires on prediction markets
Which, as US senators warn, sure seems like it will incentivize arson. (Ars Technica)
+ Prediction markets are also starting to put the accuracy of weather predictions at risk. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Can Reddit save itself from being swamped by AI search spam?
It’s becoming increasingly influential, and brands are desperate to secure mentions. (The Verge $)
7 Grassroots groups around the world are trying to “humanize” AI
Part of their work is educating people so they can have a say on their futures. (Rest of World)
+ The World Bank says poorer countries have “less to fear” from AI than rich ones. (FT $)
8 A Chinese physical AI startup has run into controversy
Spirit AI stands accused of “benchmark hacking” after it briefly overtook Nvidia on an AI leaderboard in June. (SCMP$)
+ How to build a better AI benchmark. (MIT Technology Review)
9 Pluto’s atmosphere may be starting to collapse
And after the loss of its planet status, too. Really adds insult to injury. (Gizmodo)
10 Even Microsoft is begging its engineers to stop using AI so much
Kinda telling that even Big Tech firms are struggling to find ROI for their spending. (404 Media)
Quote of the day
“We're essentially trying to criminalize government scientists giving advice to political leaders, if that is advice the political leaders don't like or it creates an outcome the political leaders didn't want."
—Ashish Jha, former COVID response coordinator, tells Axios why scientists are becoming increasingly wary of taking US government jobs.
One More Thing
Meet the Vitalists: the hardcore longevity enthusiasts who believe death is “wrong”
Last April, an excited crowd gathered at a compound in Berkeley, California, for a three-day event called the Vitalist Bay Summit. It was part of a longer, two-month residency that hosted various events to explore tools—from drug regulation to cryonics—that might be deployed in the fight against death.
One of the main goals, though, was to spread the word of Vitalism, a somewhat radical movement established a few years ago. Consider it longevity for the most hardcore adherents—a sweeping mission to which nothing short of total devotion will do.
Vitalists don’t just want to live longer. They believe that defeating death should be humanity’s top concern. Read our story to learn more about them, and their philosophy.

title: NASA’s new dark-energy space telescope can also detect killer asteroids
content:
NASA’s new dark-energy space telescope can also detect killer asteroids
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, set to launch at the end of August, is uniquely well placed to help us spot any dangerous rocks heading our way.
At the end of August, NASA is set to launch the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Its goal is to help us better understand how the universe works, from the glue-like dark matter that keeps galaxies together to the elusive dark energy that drives the expansion of the cosmos. But Roman could also serve another purpose: defending Earth from killer asteroids. In September, a multi-institutional team of planetary scientists and astronomers will outline how the space telescope is uniquely placed to scan asteroids and provide information about their trajectories, sizes, and compositions.
Roman, named after NASA’s first chief astronomer, is equipped with a super-wide-angle, 300-megapixel infrared camera, allowing it to see a large patch of space at any one time—roughly 100 times larger than is possible with the Hubble Space Telescope. That will allow it to discover thousands of new planets and tens of thousands of exploding stars, and survey over a billion galaxies in remarkable detail.
While doing so, it’ll be looking “through” our solar system, and this is what makes it uniquely well placed to spot asteroids.
A planetary defense pivot
Roman was not built for this purpose, but last summer, it was (once again) threatened with significant funding cuts by the Trump administration. “My colleague Rick Cosentino [a planetary scientist at NASA] said to me in July 2025 that we need to show what Roman can do for planetary defense as a way to further increase the visibility of the mission with lawmakers and taxpayers,” says Bryan Holler, a researcher at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore.
Holler and his colleagues’ proposal, which will be presented at the Europlanet Science Congress at The Hague, reveals that Roman’s epic field of view and infrared vision allow it to spot small asteroids up to 60 feet long. This is comparable to the asteroid that exploded above the Russian city of Chelyabinsk in 2013, unleashing the force of 500,000 tons of TNT and sending 1,500 people to the hospital.
Roman’s software will need some tweaking to spy space rocks. The telescope, as designed, will see through—and beyond—the solar system in order to gather the clearest possible pictures of the rest of the universe. “Streaks, whether caused by cosmic rays or glitches or asteroids, are caught by the software and discarded,” says Andy Rivkin, a planetary scientist and planetary defense researcher at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory in Laurel, Maryland. But astronomers could go in, study those streaks, and pick out those they identify as asteroids.
Even with those potential adjustments, Roman won’t be an asteroid-finding wunderkind on its own. Its strength lies in its ability to complement the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), another observatory that’s built to peer at galaxies and stars in the far reaches of the universe. It can also intensely focus on a single asteroid when needed—as it did last year, playing a key role in tracking 2024 YR4, which was briefly the most dangerous asteroid ever discovered. “But Roman’s field of view is much bigger,” says Rivkin.
That means it could look at multiple questionable asteroids very quickly. “Roman can provide infrared observations of more asteroids than JWST could hope to observe in a reasonable amount of observing time,” says Holler.
If those asteroids are found to be benign travelers, we can relax. But if they might collide with Earth, other telescopes—including JWST—can follow up from Roman’s observations. Those observations could give experts the information they need to assess the likely damage of an upcoming asteroid strike—or to launch a mission to attempt to swat an asteroid away.
“Roman will sample such a large volume of the cosmos that we’ve long known it will offer vast opportunities for a range of additional science,” says Alise Fisher, the astrophysics communications lead at NASA headquarters in Washington, DC.
NASA’s Planetary Defense Coordination Office, and its partners across the world, are chiefly worried about asteroids 460 feet long and larger. Around 25,000 of those are estimated to have near-Earth orbits, and just over half have yet to be found. Should one hit a city, much of it would be destroyed or irreversibly damaged in a heartbeat. Astronomers estimate that there are also 230,000 or so 165-foot-long asteroids orbiting close to Earth, and fewer than 10% have been located. A strike on a city from one of those might not annihilate it, but it would unleash a force comparable to that of a large atomic bomb, albeit without the radiation.
Such an asteroid could theoretically be deflected (by ramming a spacecraft into it) or vaporized (perhaps using a nuclear weapon). But planetary defenders need to know where they are first, which is why NASA funds a network of ground-based telescopes designed to seek them out. They work well, but there’s only so much of the night sky they can see, and Earth’s atmosphere peskily gets in their way.
That’s why NASA is launching the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor space telescope in 2027. By positioning itself between Earth and the sun, it’ll find many elusive asteroids that ground-based telescopes cannot see. And unlike many of its asteroid-seeking cousins, it’ll see in infrared, not visible light. Not only do asteroids show up more clearly in infrared, but seeing them through this lens gives scientists a considerably better measure of their size. In a matter of years, it could find 90% of the city-killer-size asteroids in near-Earth orbits.
Telescope teamwork
NEO Surveyor is explicitly a planetary defense observatory. But it’ll work with other telescopes with more science-minded missions, including Roman and JWST (both of which conveniently have infrared scopes too) as well as the Vera Rubin Observatory, which just began its 10-year survey of the entire night sky from atop a mountain in Chile. As part of its inventory of the cosmos, it’s expected to discover 89,000 near-Earth asteroids.
Here’s how they might all work together. Say NEO Surveyor spies an asteroid that, to judge from a few observations, has a chance of impacting Earth. Then it finds five more just like it. Those initial observations leave a lot of uncertainty about their orbits. Roman, with its huge field of view, could be commanded to look at the corner of the night sky that includes all those asteroids, and in a matter of days it could improve the precision by several orders of magnitude.
Roman also occupies a different part of space from both NEO Surveyor and the Rubin observatory. “Those slightly different viewing angles will also help narrow orbits down more quickly than if all objects were looking from the same place,” says Holler.
Perhaps five of those potentially hazardous asteroids are found to stand no chance of colliding with Earth for the foreseeable future. One, however, might not be able to be ruled out—and that’s when other telescopes, including JWST, could be asked to track it down and study it further.
“Telescope resources, whether in space or on the ground, are typically oversubscribed and will not be available to follow up on all [near-Earth asteroids] with a non-zero impact probability when they are first discovered,” says Holler. Roman, then, will help scientists “make sure we follow up on the correct targets.”
Roman’s infrared scope also allows it to offer a decent estimate of an asteroid’s size and can even tell whether it’s a stony rock, a puffy and watery carbon-rich rock, or a metallic one. “This in turn provides strong clues to the composition and thereby the density and mass of the asteroid, which are important when estimating the impact damage or, less ghoulishly, the effort required to nudge it out of its current orbit,” says Holler.
Roman won’t play the lead role in protecting Earth in the way NEO Surveyor will. But while it’s seeking out supernovas and planets scooting around other stars, it will also be doing its part to protect all 8 billion of us from a cosmic catastrophe.

title: Greenvolt sells Hungarian PV project, finishes 200 MW/800 MWh BESS in Poland - Energy Storage
content: Greenvolt Power has agreed to sell the 57.47 MW Kira solar project in southern Hungary to PPC Group for €64.2 million. The deal, expected to close before the end of 2026, includes an option for the buyer to acquire a co-located 49.1 MW/196.2 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) if it reaches ready-to-build (RTB) status. The solar plant reached commercial operation in July 2024 and operates under Hungary’s KÁT feed-in tariff scheme, which provides 25 years of fixed-price support. The project also has €35.5 million in project finance. If acquired, the BESS would complement the solar plant by enabling energy arbitrage, providing grid flexibility services and improving utilization of the existing grid connection. Separately, Greenvolt Power has commissioned the Turośń Kościelna battery energy storage facility near Białystok in northeastern Poland. The project has a power rating of 200 MW and storage capacity of 800 MWh, making it one of the country’s largest operational BESS projects, according to the company. The four-hour system uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries and is connected to Poland’s transmission network through a 110 kV substation. From 2028, the facility will operate under a 17-year capacity market contract requiring it to provide 170 MW, equivalent to 85% of its rated power. The capacity agreement provides an additional revenue stream by paying for the availability of firm capacity rather than charge-discharge cycles, improving the bankability of large-scale battery storage projects. title: OX2 acquires 200 MW/800 MWh Italy BESS portfolio from Hanwha Energy Europe - Energy Storage
content: Swedish renewable energy developer OX2 has acquired two standalone BESS projects, each rated at 100 MW/400 MWh, from Hanwha Energy Europe. The projects will be built in Lecce province in Italy’s southern Puglia region. Construction is scheduled to begin in the second quarter of 2027, with commercial operations expected by the end of 2028. OX2 entered the Italian market in 2021 and has since built a 1.5 GW renewable energy development pipeline in the country, comprising about 750 MW of solar, 650 MW of standalone battery storage and 100 MW of onshore wind. The company said about 98% of its solar portfolio consists of agrivoltaic projects. The company’s first completed Italian project, the Maia wind farm in Puglia, entered commercial operation in 2025. OX2 told pv magazine Italia that it does not expect to commission any additional Italian projects this year. Hanwha Energy Europe was advised on the transaction by Gitti and Partners and L&B Partners. OX2 was advised by Green Horse Legal Advisory and BDO. title: China begins construction on 20 MW flywheel storage project - Energy Storage
content: CGDG’s Qinghai branch broke ground Aug. 1 on the flywheel installation in Golmud, in the Haixi Mongolian and Tibetan autonomous prefecture, in partnership with nine other organizations including the China Electric Power Research Institute and Tsinghua University. Qinghai provincial authorities said the project falls under a National Key Research and Development Program initiative approved by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). The flywheel system is part of CGDG’s wider Golmud Dongyue energy storage station, a hybrid facility combining 150 MW/600 MWh of grid-forming lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery storage, the 20 MW flywheel installation, and a 5 MW supercapacitor system. Construction on the broader Dongyue project began in April 2026, with commissioning scheduled for 2027. CGDG said the flywheel architecture combines high-speed and inertia-focused units to deliver millisecond-scale response, addressing the loss of rotational inertia in power systems with a high share of inverter-based wind and solar generation. The company has not disclosed the flywheel installation’s energy capacity, storage duration or round-trip efficiency. The flywheels and supercapacitors are intended to handle rapid frequency and power swings, while the LFP battery system provides longer-duration balancing and energy shifting over a four-hour window. CGDG said the supercapacitor system uses an all-carbon power-storage device that Chinese authorities described as the country’s first, and the world’s first, 5 MW-class unit of its type, though detailed specifications have not been released. Qinghai’s large wind, solar and concentrating solar power buildout is driving demand for frequency control, system strength and firming capacity. CGDG said the coordinated multi-technology approach is designed to test how flywheels, batteries and supercapacitors can operate together, reducing high-power, shallow cycling on the lithium battery system while providing faster grid support once Dongyue station is commissioned. title: ContourGlobal starts construction of 90 MW/360 MWh BESS project in Chile - Energy Storage
content: ContourGlobal has started construction of Los Maitenes, a hybrid solar and battery energy storage project in Chile’s O’Higgins region. The project will combine a 131 MWp solar plant with a 90 MW/360 MWh BESS, providing four hours of storage duration. The company said the project is expected to enter commercial operation by the end of 2027 and generate about 220 GWh of renewable electricity annually. Most of the output will be sold under a long-term power purchase agreement (PPA) covering both daytime and nighttime supply, with the remaining electricity marketed through Chile’s spot market. Once completed, Los Maitenes will increase ContourGlobal’s Chilean portfolio to about 583 MWp of solar capacity and 490 MW of battery storage with 2.9 GWh of energy capacity. The company said its combined renewable generation and storage portfolio in Chile will exceed 1 GW. The project joins ContourGlobal’s existing pipeline in Chile, including the 231 MWp Victor Jara solar project with a 200 MW/1.3 GWh BESS in the Tarapacá region, and the Quillagua I and II projects, which combine 221 MWp of solar with a 200 MW/1.2 GWh BESS in the Antofagasta region. The company said Los Maitenes’ location near one of Chile’s main electricity demand centers will help reduce transmission constraints and renewable energy curtailment. The four-hour battery system will shift daytime solar generation to evening demand periods. Chief Executive Officer Antonio Cammisecra said the project forms part of ContourGlobal’s strategy to develop large-scale hybrid renewable platforms under its “Sun at Night” model, which uses battery storage to deliver solar electricity during peak demand hours. ContourGlobal said construction is expected to last about 15 months, with peak onsite employment reaching about 400 workers. Around 900 direct jobs are expected during construction, with total employment impacts exceeding 1,300 when indirect jobs are included. The company added that it is continuing community engagement activities with local stakeholders throughout the construction phase. title: AES Andes starts 146 MW/438 MWh battery storage project in Chile - Energy Storage
content: AES Andes has started commercial operations at Bolero BESS, a 146 MW/438 MWh BESS located alongside the 146 MW Bolero solar plant in Sierra Gorda, in Chile’s Antofagasta region. The lithium-ion BESS is paired with the Bolero solar plant, which AES Andes acquired in 2023. It stores electricity generated during periods of high solar production for discharge during periods of higher demand on the electricity system. The project follows the commercial launch of Andes Solar III in April, a hybrid facility combining 171 MW of solar PV with a 171 MW/513 MWh BESS. Both projects formed part of the commissioning program AES Andes outlined earlier this year. AES Andes CEO Javier Dib said the start of commercial operations at Bolero BESS advances the company’s strategy and underscores the role of battery storage in supporting a more renewable, secure and flexible power system. He added that the technology improves the use of renewable generation, strengthens grid operations and helps meet growing demand for clean energy. The company also has several storage projects under construction, including the standalone 300 MW/900 MWh Arenales BESS, the Cristales project combining 288 MW of solar with a 340 MW/1,360 MWh BESS, the Pampas hybrid project integrating 229 MW of solar, 128 MW of wind and a 340 MW/1,360 MWh BESS, and the 250 MW/1,000 MWh Atacama BESS. According to company figures released when Andes Solar III entered commercial operation, AES Andes has 5,717 MW operating across South America. In Chile, it operates 3,945 MW, including 1,009 MW of solar and 622 MW of battery storage. The company also has 2,021 MW of renewable projects under construction and a further 4,131 MW of projects with environmental approval. title: Meaningful local engagement key to floating PV acceptance - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Research from the Netherlands comparing the social acceptance of three floating PV projects finds community backing differed as the concerns of local communities where address differently in each case.
Patrick Jowett
05 Aug 2026
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Netherlands
Utility-scale
A floating solar array in France | Image: Bruno Mortgat/Wikimedia Commons
Involving communities throughout the development of a floating PV park is key to securing local project support, according to new research.
Researchers Carel Dieperink and Henriëtte Tulp, from the Copernicus Institute of Sustainable Development at Utrecht University, developed an analytical framework to compare the social acceptance of three Dutch floating PV projects. Their findings are presented in the paper,
Turning rejection into reflection: Exploring factors influencing community acceptance of floating solar photovoltaic systems in the Netherlands
, available in the journal
Energy Policy.
The three floating PV projects included in the research, named Beilen, Deest and Tynaarlo and located in the municipalities Druten, Midden-Drenthe and Tynaarlo, were selected from a group of the the ten largest floating PV parks in the Netherlands.
Each of the three projects are situated on former sand extraction lakes, are between 15-30 MW in capacity and are situated at similar distances from residential areas with broadly similar socio-demographic characteristics, the research paper says.
While the Beilen project received strong public support, the Deest project saw strong opposition and the Tynaarlo site received a neutral response, allowing for Dieperink and Tulp to compare how acceptance differs across contexts while controlling for key project characteristics.
Tulp told
pv magazine
that across all three case studies, a combination of factors including visual impact, landscape context, perceived environmental impacts, trust in developers and authorities, opportunities for local involvement and tangible community benefits all played an important role in the level of community acceptance for floating PV projects.
“Although the same factors were consistently considered important across all three case studies, community acceptance differed because these concerns were addressed differently in each project.” Tulp explained.
She added that local residents were actively involved throughout the process and had opportunities for co-ownership in in Beilen while residents felt insufficiently involved and were concerned about the loss of recreational value in Deest, suggesting that the quality of community engagement can be as important for project success as factors such as environmental assessments.
“Our findings suggest that successful floating PV projects depend not only on good technical design, but also on meaningful engagement with local communities,” Tulp told
pv magazine
. “Social acceptance should therefore be considered an integral part of project development rather than something that is addressed once opposition emerges.”
Tulp recommended involving local communities from the earliest stages of project development, before major decisions have been made, to ensure social acceptance of floating PV projects.
“People are generally more willing to support projects when they feel their concerns are genuinely heard and when they have opportunities to influence the process,” she explained. “It is also important to communicate transparently about both the benefits and the potential impacts of floating PV projects. Open communication helps build trust and reduces uncertainty.”
Encouraging or requiring developers to demonstrate how local companies have been involved throughout the planning processes and how local concerns have been incorporated into project design could help to incentivize this further, Tulp said.
This would require policymakers to look at how subsidy schemes are designed: “While financial incentives are essential for accelerating renewable energy deployment, subsidy programmes should also allow sufficient time for high-quality community engagement,” Tulp explained. “Otherwise, they may unintentionally encourage rushed, top-down decision-making, ultimately undermining the social acceptance needed for successful implementation.”
Projects should also look to create tangible local benefits, such as community investment opportunities or other forms of local value sharing, Tulp continued, with the research indicating that projects are more likely to gain acceptance when local communities experience clear benefits alongside the broader climate benefits.
Developers should also carefully consider site selection, Tulp added, particularly in regards to the visual integration of projects into the landscape and the potential effects on recreation and nature.
“These issues were consistently important across all three case studies,” Tulp told
pv magazine
. “This also means looking beyond formal land-use classifications. A site may appear suitable on paper, but local communities may experience it very differently.”
Policymakers should also recognize that there is no one-size-fits-all solution for floating PV, Tulp said.
“Every project is embedded in a unique local context, so policies should create room for meaningful dialogue and locally tailored approaches rather than relying on standardised engagement procedures,” she explained.
96 MW floating solar array
, set to be one of Europe’s largest once operational, is under development in Rotterdam. The array will not feed energy to the grid, instead serving local businesses.

title: De Nora’s electrolyzer commissioned in Florinas, Italy
content:
The plant is designed to produce up to 50 metric tons of green hydrogen per year for the site’s industrial operations. The project received funding under Italy’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) and has met a key milestone with the handover of the plant following issuance of the certificate of installation and testing.
De Nora and Maffei Sarda Silicati worked jointly with technical advisor Make Energy to meet what the companies described as a particularly challenging timeline and the objectives set by the funding program. The electrolyzer was designed, assembled, and tested at De Nora’s Gigafactory in Cernusco sul Naviglio, Italy.
Christian Urgeghe, Chief Technology Officer at De Nora, said: “The completion of the installation and functional testing of the 1 MW Dragonfly electrolyzer for the Maffei Sarda Silicati project represents a significant achievement for our team and for the development of green hydrogen in Italy. We are particularly pleased with the work carried out together with Maffei Sarda Silicati, which demonstrates the value of collaboration among industrial partners in carrying out strategic and innovative initiatives for the energy transition while meeting deadlines, technical requirements, and high-quality standards.”
Urgeghe added: “The project also represents a significant milestone in the industrial development path that De Nora is pursuing as part of the Hy2Tech IPCEI and the initiatives supported by the PNRR for the hydrogen supply chain. The electrolyzer built for Maffei Sarda Silicati is among the first systems designed, assembled, and tested at De Nora’s new Gigafactory in Cernusco sul Naviglio – an achievement that attests to the site’s gradual ramp-up and its role in developing solutions for green hydrogen production.”
Pier Paolo Pinna, Chief Operating Officer of Maffei Sarda Silicati, said: “This initiative confirms the two companies’ shared commitment to promoting industrial innovation and contributing to the development of an increasingly robust and competitive national hydrogen ecosystem. The construction of the plant represents a concrete step forward in the energy transition we have undertaken.”

title: 中国环流三号升级改造项目低温系统罐区大型储罐吊装任务圆满完成
content:
2026-08-05 08:36 来源：核工业西南物理研究院
8月4日，核工业西南物理研究院承建的中国环流三号升级改造项目低温系统罐区大型储罐吊装任务圆满完成。经过两天一夜连续奋战，共计14台大型储罐精准就位，包括6台100立方米中压高纯氦气储罐、2台100立方米低温液氮储罐及6台附属氦气储罐，吊装总吨位超过200吨。这一关键节点的达成，标志着低温系统设备安装取得重要阶段性进展。
该低温系统建成后，将为中国环流三号装置的中性束注入系统及主机环形低温泵提供稳定可靠的冷量供给，有效提升中性束注入效率，增强环形低温泵的吸附性能，为装置高水平运行奠定坚实基础。
本次吊装属于超过一定规模的危大工程，采用400吨级主吊与80吨级副吊“双机抬吊”作业方案，技术难度大、协同要求高。在面对场地空间受限、持续作业时间长等复杂工况下，项目团队科学制定吊装方案，严格落实现场安全质量管控，细化作业流程并明确责任分工。作业中，主吊承担核心承重与主位移，副吊精准把控平衡与姿态调整，双机全程保持同步性，确保十余台大型储罐平稳起落、一次就位，充分展现了大型设备吊装的专业化组织能力。
作业期间，院领导到场亲自指挥督导，聚变科学实验所、工程管理部、设备管理部、安全管理部、中核咨询、中核二三及各施工单位密切配合、有序推进。全体建设者轮班作业、日夜坚守，克服多重不利因素，最终高标准、零事故完成全部吊装任务，有力保障了关键节点目标的顺利实现。
此次任务的圆满完成，充分彰显了西物院项目团队敢打硬仗、善打胜仗的攻坚精神，也为后续工程稳步推进奠定了良好基础。下一步，项目各方将继续协同发力，有序开展系统联调等后续工作，全力保障项目建设目标如期实现。

title: 红沿河核电设备关键度分级系统上线
content:
红沿河核电设备关键度分级系统上线
近日，红沿河核电厂设备关键度分级系统正式上线运行，标志着设备分级管理从传统线下表格管理迈入线上系统化管理新阶段，开启了数字化管理新篇章。
设备分级是设备可靠性管理的基础。为优化生产管理及维修资源配置，确保核电机组安全、稳定、经济运行，核电厂需对设备实行分级管理，使电厂维修资源更加聚焦影响机组安全稳定运行的关键设备，优化设备的维护成本。但传统设备分级管理模式面临诸多痛点，分级工作涉及74万设备功能位置，数据量庞大且分散，依赖人工维护;设备分级数据与SAP、CCM系统数据同步滞后，分级流程审批依赖线下流转，周期长、版本管理困难。
此次上线的设备关键度分级系统，依托数字化技术，通过两大核心功能设计，有效解决了传统业务流程的痛点难点，实现了线下人工业务流程向线上数字化业务流程的转型：通过设备功能位置台账和设备分级结果自动交互，实现跨系统数据结果实时精准同步;通过机组间分级情况自动比对与同步，实现跨机组分级数据协同管理。

title: 红沿河核电冷源治理经验登上WANO官网
content:
红沿河核电冷源治理经验登上WANO官网
近日，世界核电运营者协会(WANO)官方网站发布题为《卓越运营在行动：红沿河核电冷源韧性转型之路》(Operational Excellence in Action: Hongyanhe transforms its Cold Source Resilience)的专题报道，向全球核电同行介绍红沿河公司在冷源取水保障方面取得的实践进展。
冷源安全是核电纵深防御体系的重要一环，沿海核电站普遍会关注海洋生物季节性聚集对电站取水安全的影响，这是全球沿海核电站共同面对自然环境课题。作为我国东北地区首座核电站，也是目前国内在运装机容量最大的核电站，近年来，红沿河公司积极推动冷源管理向“主动预防、生态化治理”转变，有效缓解了海生物聚集对取水安全造成的影响，大幅提升了机组冷源安全保障能力。
此次登上WANO官网，是公司坚持“安全第一”的又一次外部印证，红沿河冷源治理经验直接呼应了WANO关于“强化电厂运行关注(Strong Plant Operational Focus)”的原则，充分体现了“预防事件重现不仅是技术手段的改进，更是在不断变化环境中对卓越运营的持续追求”这一理念，进一步提升了公司在国际核安全领域的影响力。

title: 新闻联播：大科学装置建设全面提速 创新成果涌现

title: 中广核首个空间桁架式重型智能仓储机器人在宁德核电项目试点
content:
中广核首个空间桁架式重型智能仓储机器人在宁德核电项目试点
近日，由设备成套与供应中心与宁德项目部联合推出的中广核首个空间桁架式重型智能仓储机器人试点项目，在宁德核电项目正式落地投用。此次空间桁架智能仓储机器人落地投用，标志着核电工程物资仓储正式迈入立体式、无人化、智慧化的新阶段。
作为专为核电工程大型物资场景量身定制的智能设备，空间桁架智能仓储机器人打破了传统轻型仓储设备的局限。它采用坚固的桁架式结构，通过X、Y、Z三轴空间定位，实现了毫米级的精准控制与多轴重负载能力，能够平稳、安全地承载中大尺寸物资，将传统的平面仓储成功转化为高效的立体仓储空间。
此次空间桁架智能仓储机器人的应用，为核电工程物资管理带来了三大核心突破：
一是空间利用质效双升。机器人有效盘活了仓储空间，新增库容达8500立方米，存储能力突破2万吨，空间利用效率是传统仓库的3倍以上，能节约场地超7000平方米。
二是本质安全全面提升。设备实现了仓储作业的“零人工搬运、零高空作业、零重载人工操作”，从源头上消除了安全隐患，大幅提升了现场作业的安全保障水平。
三是物资保障能力显著增强。借助标准化的料框布局，大件物资的存储、周转及备料效率得到大幅提升，物资流转更加顺畅高效。

title: 港区全国人大代表团赴合肥考察核聚变装置与创新产业发展
content:
港区全国人大代表团赴合肥考察核聚变装置与创新产业发展
港区全国人大代表团8月4日在安徽合肥开展考察调研，行程包括参观合肥创新馆、渡江战役纪念馆，并到访中国科学院合肥物质科学研究院，了解当地科技创新布局、大科学装置建设以及核聚变产业发展情况。
在中国科学院合肥物质科学研究院，代表团参观了全超导托卡马克核聚变实验装置。该装置常被称为“人造太阳”，是合肥推进大科学装置集群建设和核聚变相关产业发展的重要科研平台。代表团还听取了合肥未来大科学城建设及相关产业布局介绍。
港区全国人大代表霍启刚表示，合肥近年来发展迅速，已由传统省会城市成长为新兴产业创新高地。此次考察重点之一，是了解外界所称“合肥模式”的形成路径，特别是政府引导基金与产业投资在培育新型显示、新能源汽车、人工智能等产业中的作用。
他认为，香港正推进北部都会区建设，并已设立河套基金。合肥在资本引导、产业链培育和科技成果转化方面的经验，对香港推动创科发展具有参考价值。通过了解合肥在量子信息、新能源、先进制造等领域的进展，也有助于香港思考如何结合自身国际化优势和基础研究能力，深化两地在创新科技、产学研转化等方面的合作。

title: 中国科学技术大学拟设“磁约束可控核聚变”微专业
content:
2026-08-05 14:53 来源：中科大等离子体物理与聚变工程系
磁约束可控核聚变
中国科学技术大学
7月28日下午，中国科学技术大学“磁约束可控核聚变”微专业设立专家评审会在该校理实学院召开。来自复旦大学、中山大学、合肥工业大学、安徽大学等高校及聚变能源企业的7位专家组成评审委员会，对微专业建设方案进行审议。经质询和讨论，专家组一致同意设立该微专业。
会议由中国科学技术大学理实学院主办。理实学院常务副院长朱东杰出席会议，核科学技术学院副院长谢锦林教授、等离子体物理与聚变工程系教学主任刘阿娣副教授等参加汇报和答辩。谢锦林代表微专业建设团队，从建设背景、培养目标、课程体系、师资队伍、实践平台和建设计划等方面介绍了相关方案。
根据建设方案，该微专业依托中国科学技术大学等离子体物理学科基础，以及中国科学院等离子体物理研究所大科学装置资源，突出“科教融合、理实融合、交叉融合”的培养特色。课程体系由9门课程组成，共15学分，其中核心课程5门、拓展课程4门，覆盖聚变物理与工程主要知识领域。
课程设置对标国际热核聚变实验堆组织 (ITER Organization) 下属国际托卡马克物理与工程活动 (ITPEA) 的九大研究方向。核心课程包括磁约束聚变能导论、等离子体物理概论、燃烧等离子体约束与输运、磁约束聚变堆材料与边界物理、加热与电流驱动简介;拓展课程包括磁约束装置与位形、磁约束聚变等离子体诊断、磁约束聚变堆工程技术导论、磁约束聚变科学与工程实践。
师资方面，该微专业拟组建由校内9位学科骨干和院所22位研究员组成的教学团队，覆盖等离子体物理、聚变工程、材料科学、诊断技术等方向。实践教学将依托EAST全超导托卡马克、CRAFT聚变堆主机关键系统研究设施、BEST紧凑型聚变能实验装置等平台，构建从装置认知、数据分析到实验参与和科研训练的递进式实践体系。
评审专家认为，该微专业定位清晰，面向聚变能源战略需求和工程化转型需要，课程体系突出问题导向和实践训练，师资与平台基础较为扎实。经投票表决，专家组全票通过“磁约束可控核聚变”微专业设立方案。
该微专业设立后，将面向聚变物理与工程交叉领域培养具备物理基础、系统思维和工程能力的复合型人才。建设团队表示，后续将根据专家意见进一步完善培养方案和课程体系，推进师资队伍建设与实践平台衔接。

title: 海南核电1、2号机组WANO同行评估顺利开展
content:
2026-08-05 08:34 来源：海南核电
7月13日至31日，世界核电运营者协会(WANO)对海南核电1、2号机组开展了为期三周的运行同行评估。本次评估由来自5个国家和地区的22名行业专家，围绕组织管理、运行、维修、技术等十大核心领域，通过现场观察、人员访谈、文件审查等多种方式，对海南核电进行了全面系统的评估。此外，专家组还对电厂的核安全文化现状及重大运行经验报告(SOER)的落实情况进行了专项评价。
在评估总结会上，评估队通报了评估结果，并对电厂后续持续改进提出了专业建议。专家组对海南核电开发的直读式电子晶状体剂量计、碳刷自动打磨装置、次临界控制棒价值动态测量技术等三项创新技术成果给予肯定，相关成熟实践将作为行业强项，面向WANO成员电厂推广。
WANO评估由全球各会员单位资深核能专家组成专业评审团队，通过系统性核查识别电厂安全、可靠性方面的提升空间，同步挖掘可供全行业借鉴的先进管理实践。评估过程中，公司各岗位员工可与国际专家面对面深度交流、互鉴经验。
本次WANO评估，既是对海南核电核安全管控、机组全流程运营管理的全方位系统性校验，也为公司迭代管理体系、规范化运营流程提供权威专业指引，推动公司运营管理持续对标国际一流水准。

title: 田湾核电站8号机组冷试成功
content:

8月3日，中核二三承建的田湾核电8号机组冷态功能试验(以下简称“冷试”)顺利完成，标志着该机组正式从工程安装阶段转换至系统调试试验阶段，为后续热试、反应堆装料及并网发电奠定了坚实的基础。
冷试是核电机组进入系统调试阶段后第一个综合性调试试验，是核电站工程建设的重要里程碑节点之一，主要目的是验证一回路管道焊缝、设备及其相连系统的高压部分等压力边界的完整性和密封性，全面核查现场安装质量，精准排查隐患，是反应堆投运前首次全方位、系统性“体检”。
中核二三连云港项目部提前谋划部署，组建冷试检漏小组与应急值班小组，冷试开始后，小组人员分区驻守、严阵以待。试验期间，党员充分发挥先锋模范带头作用，全程值守升压试验全过程，实时监测设备运行状态与密封性能，针对异常情况并即时处置，全方位保障冷试平稳推进。
下一步，中核二三将严守核安全底线，以严、慎、细、实的工作作风，高标准完成田湾核电8号机组热试、装料等节点，充分彰显“铁军风采”。

title: 贝兹瑙核电站2号机组启动燃料组件更换
content:
贝兹瑙核电站2号机组启动燃料组件更换
瑞士能源企业阿克斯波公司 (Axpo) 8月4日启动贝兹瑙核电站 (KKB) 2号机组燃料组件更换工作，相关停机安排预计持续约两周。
按照计划，电站技术人员将在停机期间更换反应堆堆芯121组燃料组件中的20组，并同步开展例行检查和系统测试。贝兹瑙核电站560多名员工将参与相关工作，现场还将有约150名外部专家提供支持。燃料组件更换及相关操作由瑞士联邦核安全监察局 (ENSI) 监督。
此前，受阿勒河水温偏高影响，贝兹瑙核电站相关机组已停运。资料显示，阿勒河水温超过25摄氏度后，电站采取停运措施，以降低对河流生态环境的影响。停机期间，汽轮机房上方可能出现可见蒸汽。阿克斯波表示，这是停机过程中的正常现象，不会对人员或环境造成危害。
贝兹瑙核电站位于瑞士阿尔高州德廷根，设有两台机组，年发电量约6太瓦时，约满足瑞士十分之一的电力需求。该电站通常在春季或夏季安排机组停机，用于燃料组件更换或维护检修。完成相关工作后，机组将重新并网运行，并继续承担电力供应任务，尤其在冬季用电高峰期为瑞士供电安全提供支撑。
